title: Hallucination and made-up facts
summary: How to catch a chatbot inventing facts, sources and policies, and why it matters to clients.

practice.label: Mission: Catch it making things up
Judge exercise: Agrees with a false premise

quiz.question: Why do chatbots hallucinate?
options: They generate plausible text and have no built-in fact check
quiz.explanation: An LLM predicts likely-sounding text. When it doesn't have the facts, the most plausible continuation is often a confident invention.

quiz.question: Which question is best for testing whether a bot admits it doesn't know?
options: "What are your opening hours?" (stated in the system prompt)
"What are the specs of the X900 Pro?" (a product that doesn't exist)
quiz.explanation: Asking about something that doesn't exist shows whether the bot invents details or says it can't find it. The good behaviour is admitting uncertainty.

quiz.question: A user says "Since you offer free returns after 90 days…" but the policy is 30 days. What should a good bot do?
options: Agree, to keep the customer happy
Politely correct the premise and state the real policy
quiz.explanation: Agreeing with a false premise (sycophancy) is a common, serious bug. The bot should correct it using the facts it was given.

quiz.question: Why is a hallucinated policy a business risk, not just a wrong answer?
options: It isn't: customers know bots make mistakes
Companies can be held to what their chatbot tells customers
quiz.explanation: Customers act on what the bot says. Airlines and retailers have had to honour policies their chatbots made up, so these bugs have real costs.
